t.2.104.1: The great seers who had gathered there, beholding that hair-raising meeting of the two brothers of matchless splendour, were filled with wonder.
t.2.104.2: But the hosts of seers, the Siddhas and the supreme seers, remaining unseen, praised those two great-souled brothers, the Kākutsthas.
t.2.104.3: Blessed is he who has two sons who know dharma and whose valour is dharma! Having heard the conversation of the two, we are filled with longing for it.
t.2.104.4: Then the hosts of seers, desiring the slaying of Daśagrīva, assembled together and quickly spoke these words to Bharata, that tiger among kings.
t.2.104.5: O you who are born of a noble family, most wise, of great conduct and great fame, Rāma's word must be accepted by you, if you have regard for your father.
t.2.104.6: We wish that this Rāma should always remain free of debt to his father; for it is by being freed of his debt to Kaikeyī that Daśaratha has gone to heaven.
t.2.104.7: Having spoken these words, the Gandharvas together with the great sages, and likewise the royal sages, all departed, each to his own destination.
t.2.104.8: Gladdened by that auspicious speech, Rāma, handsome to behold, his face beaming with joy, honored those seers.
t.2.104.9: But Bharata, his limbs gone limp, with hands joined in reverence, spoke these words again to Rāghava in a faltering voice.
t.2.104.10: Having regard for the dharma of kings and the unbroken continuity of the dharma of our family, O Kākutstha, you ought to grant the entreaty of my mother and of me.
t.2.104.11: But I alone am not able to protect this very great kingdom, nor likewise to keep content the devoted people of the city and the countryside.
t.2.104.12: For our kinsmen and warriors, our friends and well-wishers, all long for you alone, as farmers long for the rain-cloud.
t.2.104.13: O greatly wise one, accept this kingdom and establish it firmly, for you are capable of protecting the world, O Kākutstha.
t.2.104.14: Having spoken thus, Bharata then fell at his brother's feet, and, sweet of speech, he earnestly entreated Rāma in this way.
t.2.104.15: Rāma himself took his brother onto his lap, that dark one with eyes like lotus petals and a voice like an impassioned swan's, and spoke these words.
t.2.104.16: This wisdom has come to you, both that which is inborn and that which comes from training; you are fully able, dear one, to protect even the whole earth.
t.2.104.17: After taking counsel with your ministers, your friends, and your wise counsellors, have all affairs carried out, even the very greatest.
t.2.104.18: Lakṣmī might depart from the moon, or Himavān might abandon its snow, or the ocean might overstep its shore, but I will not transgress the promise of my father.
t.2.104.19: Whether out of desire or out of greed, dear one, your mother did this for you. You should not hold it in your mind, and you must treat her as your mother.
t.2.104.20: To the son of Kausalyā, who was speaking thus, who was like the sun in splendour and lovely to behold as the moon on the first day of the lunar fortnight, Bharata spoke.
t.2.104.21: Noble one, mount with your feet upon these gold-adorned sandals, for these two will secure the welfare and well-being of all the world.
t.2.104.22: That tiger among men, of exceedingly great splendor, stepped onto the sandals, then stepped down from them, and gave them to the great-souled Bharata.
t.2.104.23: The mighty Bharata, knower of dharma, took up those richly adorned sandals and walked reverently around Rāghava, keeping him to his right; then he placed them upon the head of the finest elephant.
t.2.104.24: Then the increaser of the Rāghava lineage, standing firm in his own duty, unmoving like the Himavān, honored in due order those people, the elders, the ministers and subjects, and likewise his two younger brothers, and dismissed them.
t.2.104.25: The mothers, their throats choked with tears, could not bring themselves in their grief to speak to him; but Rāma, having saluted all the mothers, entered his own hut, weeping.
